text_original: Ive heard enough incidences of EVs having problems in rain puddles, random critical alerts, battery mileage decreasing over time, battery problems leading to expensive replacements, accidental fires and an overall higher cost of ownership, to not ever consider buying one. Most companies provide battery warranty for only 8 years or 1,60,000km. The question is what will happen after that ? I'll tell you what happens. You spend 1/3rd to 1/2th the price of the car for a replacement, and you'd be lucky if they even give you an original previously unused battery. These cars also can't be maintained the way ICE engines can. A yearly good cleaning (engine flush), engine oil replacement, oil filter and air filter replacement and your car is as good as new barring this is done every year. EVs however don't have these components, so if your battery is dying or becoming weak, this is not something that can be dealt with in a normal service. You get the battery either replaced or you'll essentially be left with an overly expensive frame with wheels sitting at your home. Lastly any person having the capability to buy either an ICE or an EV makes enough money and doesn't have so much time on hand to plug the ev into a damn charger in case an important meeting or emergency. No such bs with an ICE vehicle tho, you refuel within minutes and go about your business. Always remember, you buy the car for convenience not to plug it and wait for hours. It's also worth mentioning that the amounts of lithium and other metals required for their production, raises more pollution that all of the ICE vehicles will ever do combined. Not to mention the electricity needed to charge isn't as green as you might think especially in India. Most of it comes from thermal power plants which use coal for generating electricity. Maybe in the future EVs will be the standard but as of now, that future is looking bleak to say the least.

text_original: I observed few issues, apart from the mentioned list. Hope this helps. 1. ADAS: Auto Emergency Steering automatically steers towards ongoing traffic, if someone tries to overtake us from back. It can not be permanently disabled. 2. ADAS: Static objects such as 'Police barricades' or 'Traffic cones' are not detected. Vehicle crashed on to them. 3. Fast Charging: Maximum charging speed is limited to 88kW and not 180kW as advertised. 4. No safe audio defaults possible. It always restores previous volumes. If you had low volume on Bluetooth and had set volume high, on next start you will have a shockingly high volume from FM, until Bluetooth is connected. We can not change anything for at least 20 sec, as shown in the video. 5. Secure 360 is almost useless. It does not do 24x7 recording even with a 128GB Pen drive in DVR port. It only records random events, which are almost useless every time. It failed to record an auto hitting me from side, a bicycle crossing me from front, which were very crucial. Also, it does not recycle old recordings if internal storage is full, it simply stops saving new recordings. 6. User Profiles feature is announced but still not available. 7. 'Door Open Cabin Lights On' switch does not save the state. It always goes to OFF, for every restart. 8. Android Auto completely overtakes the full screen. It takes a minimum of 3 careful touches to come to Mahindra Home screen, which is very risky, when driving. 9. Android Auto is connected by default, if paired. There is no way to control this behaviour. 10. Mobile App logs out very frequently (once or twice every week). This is highly annoying. 11. There is no way to select default drive mode. For example, we can not set 'Everyday' or 'Range' mode as default, as there is a separate default mode. BTW, I reported all these issues to Mahindra long back, but to no avail. They either do not acknowledge or simply dismiss them as 'by design'

text_original: I own a Ioniq 5 and I agree with most of the positives and negatives. Tons of room (in the EU we consider this car to be really huge), smooth driving and great general comfort. The car is loaded with stuff like automatic parking and steering assist, my main gripe is that those systems are a clear "version 1". Steering help works but pulls on the steering wheel at random, automatic parking takes forever and does not park the car within the parking space. That sort of thing. Driving wise: excellent car. And for app connectivity: Bluelink was slow and bad, they replaced it with My Hyundai which is also slow but otherwise a lot better. I still think that maintenance cost is low, except for the coolant flush and the e-call battery replacement (~$600, but that may be a EU-only thing). As long as your ECCU doesn't die, this is a very reliable car with manageable maintenance cost. The blue coolant has low electrical conductivity, and is only used for battery cooling. Over time, the anti-static properties dissipate. If you don't change it in time, it could cause electrical issues within the battery pack. Newer Ioniq 5 from 2024 don't have the blue coolant anymore, so apparently this conductivity thing has not really been an issue. If you want to keep your warranty, you have to flush the blue coolant in earlier models. My car has done 100000 km (about 62000 miles), so far so good. The ECCU still works (there was a recall), and the car is still on the original (!) Michelin tires. A couple of weeks ago, the pink coolant seems to have started leaking, that should be fixed next week within warranty. That's what 5 years of warranty does. Let's see what the next 60000 miles will bring me.

text_original: I have a 2020 Hyundai IONIQ EV. The IONIQ 5 is absolutely my next vehicle. However currently, I have had an issue for a year now that Hyundai can't seemingly fix. When temperatures rise above 60F, I get a wonderful refill coolant light despite fluid levels being perfect. When I purchased it, the light was not on, yet within a few weeks, there it was. I bought it during some relatively cool weather, so due to that, I missed the issue at purchase that would of killed the sale. I've taken it in for this issue and they did a full coolant flush, changed out the coolant pumps, then changed some internal sensors and still the light is on. Mind you these things were performed on 3 seperate visits which took every bit of 6 weeks total. My last visit after the light was still on, I was told they are ordering a new coolant pipe. As you could probably guess, they never called me back to schedule my 4th appointment and that was about 8 months ago. I'm now at 46,000 miles, a meer 4k away from my warranty being used up at 50k or the 5 year mark. It's sad that even though I know the work needed to fix the issue is going to be free, I'm dreading the wait and run around the Hyundai employees give. The dealership to customer relationship is non existent. They are the worst by far in terms of communication and customer concerns. They act as if everyone has additional vehicles they can drive while your car sits in their parking lot for a week before it's even touched. Only to find out nothing has been actually fixed. Sure I got a couple free parts and a coolant flush, but the entire reason I brought it in to begin with remains. It's almost as if they are trained to tag you along just long enough to allow your warranty to run out. Some of you may think, what's the big deal about a dash light? Well this particular one isn't some semi discreet corner light on the dash. It's a full blown warning that encompasses the center of the speedometer screen, which constantly beeps and flashes red if you touch anything. Turn on windshield wipers, warning tone. Change radio stations, warning tone. Check messages, warning tone. Etc etc. It doesn't disappear nor can it be dismissed as it's classified as a critical warning. Other than that issue, I absolutely love the car. Hyundai's development team really hit the mark on these vehicles. While not as quick as the IONIQ 5, the torque of the 2020 is more than enough to get up and go. If by some odd reason they cannot fix this dash light issue with their current methods, I've read case reports to where they have had to replace the entire battery pack to resolve the issue. I'm willing to go that far if need be, but it's probably going to be a battle to achieve it. I hope anyone on the fence about purchasing one, realizes these vehicles and their price point is amazing for what you get. But do keep in mind the employees are not necessarily going to very helpful if something occurs. text_original: I already have a love-hate relationship with my '23 Ioniq5 Limited and I've barely owned it for a month. Finding operational charging stations when traveling in Pennsylvania has been a real problem (even in Metro areas). Sometimes charging simply stops after a minute (though I don't know if it's the car or the station or a combination of the two -- it works fine for me at home). The navigation system is generally a mess. You can turn the navigation volume down to zero but it will still pause the car audio when it noiselessly speaks. The best audio system they offer - Bose I think - is surprisingly awful. I don't like the controls or algorithm for the adaptive cruise control at all. Some of the steering wheel buttons are really flimsy. Having 4 regeneration levels + i-Pedal (single pedal driving) + a "let the car decide" mode gives you a lot of flexibility. But Level 3 is jerky when accelerating/braking at low speeds so I use 2. My '23 Chevy Bolt costs half as much as has superior one-pedal-driving, not to mention a better user interface, but that's just my opinion. Much of the Ioniq manual seems like it was translated from Korean by someone who isn't fluent in English, which made it difficult to understand all the different regeneration settings. But the power and sporty handling are great. The seats are very comfortable for me. The "overhead" camera view helps me park perfectly between the lines (which I'm not very good at). I'm curious whether I'll be able to power a fridge in my garage from the car battery next time my house power goes out. It hasn't needed service yet. With my Bolt I just waited until the car reached the next 15K interval (I'd bought it used) and then I had the tires rotated and the wiper blades changed. I hope the Hyundai will be that easy.

text_original: I drive a 2024 base model Ioniq 5. Bought it in Aug 2025 for $24K. The best thing about it is the driving experience: quiet, smooth, with a ton of acceleration when needed. The rear camera includes side-sensors to detect traffic cross-traffic behind me--a HUGE plus in parking lots. But I do have several bones to pick with the car: 1. No rear windshield wiper--a MAJOR annoyance, and a stupid omission. 2. Crappy (to put it politely) plastic trim pieces on wheel wells, which are totally unnecessary and break off with contact with ANYTHING. In the one year I've owned the car, I've had to replace both front trim pieces due to contact with snow/ice piles in winter--and they are not cheap. They shouldn't even be there; it should be fender metal all the way to the edge of the wheel well. 3. Crappy wheel well liner/trim assembly: plastic wheel well liners are attached to the aforementioned plastic trim with plastic fasteners, and the whole assembly is in turn attached to the fender with more plastic fasteners. I've had to replace both front wheel well liners in addition to the trim, after they broke off after brushing against snow/ice piles. Cheap cheap cheap! 4. Crappy front and rear bumper covers. The plastic is low grade and brittle; any contact with any object will cause them to crack. I already have visible cracks front and back. Thank goodness for black Gorilla Tape. 5. The biggest issue is the 12V battery. Hyundai is known for putting crappy 12Vs in their cars, and the 2024 Ioniq 5 is no exception. It only comes with a 12mo/12Kmi warranty, but I've had to replace the 12V twice already, in 12 months. Luckily the local dealership replaced it under warranty both times, but still. And there's no battery charge indicator, so you get no warning: out of the blue you get a "low 12V battery charge" error on the display, leaving you dead in the water, since the car won't start if the 12V is low. ***AT ALL***. Which really sucks, big time. This is where that small frunk comes in handy: it's where you store the $80 li-ion jump-starter that you are definitely going to need. The car can be jump-started with cables, like a normal ICE vehicle, and it only takes a few seconds, but if you don't have another vehicle handy, the little jump-starter battery is a life-saver. And of course that small storage area under the rear deck is perfect for jumper cables. Bottom line, Hyundai really needs to upgrade their 12V battery game. One caveat on those li-ion jump starters: don't forget--like I did--to charge them every three months or so. I forgot about mine and left it in the frunk for 8 months, which left it dead--permanently. Had to replace it. But FTR, my 2024 base model does in fact have the automatic rear liftgate. Also FTR, I think the car is ugly as sin, but I have never bought a car for its looks. Despite all these complaints, I don't regret buying this car. It's comfy and a pleasure to drive, and has decent range: 300 to 330 miles in warm weather, though cold weather does bring a hefty penalty, as do heater, AC, and high speed. If you want to range-max, the sweet spot seems to be around 55 MPH on the highway.

Here are a few key points you may want to include: 1. Charging Model: - Charging an EV via external DC fast chargers or public stations is not a sustainable long-term model. - The ideal and most efficient way is home charging, especially using a night-time charger while you sleep. You wake up to a fully charged car every day, with minimal cost and maximum convenience. 2. Running Costs: - Charging from external sources (DC chargers, commercial setups) is more expensive than home charging, but still cheaper than petrol or diesel for long-distance driving. - Per-kilometer running costs remain in favor of EVs, especially for users covering longer distances regularly. 3. Cost Comparison – EV vs Petrol/Diesel: - Always compare the top-end EV with the top model petrol/diesel variant of the same car (if available). This gives a fair pricing perspective. - Often, the price difference for similarly specced models isn’t much. In such cases, go for the EV – it offers better value in the long run. - However, lower-cost EV variants (₹18–24 lakh bracket) may not offer the best value for money when you consider features and practicality. This is subjective but can be a deal-breaker for many. 4. Three-Phase Power is Crucial: - For home chargers (7.2kW to 11kW), a three-phase connection is highly recommended. - While Maharashtra Electricity Board (MSEB) does cap usage at 5kW, in practice, a full home load test (e.g., geyser, fridge, oven, AC, lights, etc.) can draw over 32kW during peak usage. - With three-phase supply, you can distribute the load, avoiding overloads and ensuring safe operation. - Newer constructions (past 3–4 years) typically come with three-phase setups by default, in anticipation of solar energy systems. For older buildings, even if you pay MSEB to upgrade, it may not be effective beyond updating the meter cap from 5kW to 11kW. 5. Installation Costs: - Yes, cable installation costs from your meter to the parking spot are your responsibility. ( NOC from Society in Buliding is not Deal Breaker you will get it ) - The farther your parking, the more you pay. - For example, Tata provides 15 meters of cable for free. Beyond that, they charge approx. ₹621 per meter. Costs may vary for other brands. - These are initial setup investments that need to be made if you want to enjoy the low long-term costs of EV ownership. this are Trade of.

text_original: If you are planning to buy an Ather scooter, please think twice. The scooter may look premium, but the after-sales support is extremely poor and unreliable. It has been only 4 months since I bought the scooter and the belt has already come off and started slipping. I had already given the scooter for its first service, expecting that any issue would be checked and fixed. But the service center failed to diagnose anything and returned it saying “everything is fine, all parts are good.” Soon after, the issue became serious. When I took it back, I was told to wait 5 days because they do not have the belt in stock. The scooter has now been lying in the service center for 2 days, and I still have no update, no response, no urgency. If this is happening within 4 months, I genuinely fear what more problems I will have to face in the coming months and years. And more importantly, how many excuses I will have to listen to from the service team. At this rate, I don’t know how many days, weeks, or even months the scooter will have to spend in the service center each time something goes wrong. If this is your only vehicle, you will suffer. You will be left stuck, waiting, and helpless — because service support is slow, careless, and uncommitted. It clearly feels like Ather is only bothered about selling their scooters, not about supporting customers after purchase. Honestly, traditional petrol bikes are far more reliable. They don’t make you regret your investment. Think very carefully before choosing Ather. The real problems begin after the purchase, and that’s where Ather fails the most.

text_original: At a price of ₹1.5 lakh+, the TVS iQube S feels like a complete disappointment. The overall build quality is very poor, and cheap materials have been used throughout. The charger comes with only a 6-month warranty, and if it stops working, you’ll have to spend around ₹12,000 for a new one. Considering all this, the scooter feels overpriced and impractical. In comparison, a petrol scooter like the Activa costs around ₹1 lakh, is reliable, easy to maintain, and has decent resale value.
